The seed library in Kharkhoda's panchayat hall was only a steel cupboard and a register, but forty families now swapped seeds there each sowing season. Simran had built it over two years. Now the nursing post in the district hospital was hers, and she would be there six days a week.
Sitting on the hall steps, she counted on her fingers. Who opens the cupboard in June when I'm on a night shift? Who writes in the register? Who buys the paper packets when they run out?
Arnab, the dairy man's son, had helped her sort millet seeds every Saturday. That week she stood beside him while he filled the register himself. Then she went to the milk cooperative meeting and asked if a small share of each month's fund could buy packets and ink. The members agreed.
"Now it belongs to the village," Arnab said.

School log, Thursday.
Mr Shankar came today to see the lab he gave us last June. Twelve computers, new tables, a banner with his company's name. The room has been locked since Diwali. Power comes for about four hours a day here, mostly after school, and there is no inverter. None of our teachers has used these machines before, so nobody felt confident to take a class in there.
I unlocked it for him. Dust covers on every screen. A few Class 6 children pressed their faces to the window glass as we stood inside.
He was quiet for a long time, then asked why nobody had told him. I said we did not want to seem ungrateful.

Went back to Bhimpur school today, first time since we opened the lab in March. I was carrying the photo from the opening ceremony on my phone. All ten tablets charging, children smiling.

On the first Monday of every month, Priscila spread three sheets across the kitchen table of the community flat in Porto. Attendance from the sign-in book. The short maths quiz the children took each Friday. And the feedback cards, where they drew a face and wrote one sentence.
Ulla, the volunteer who ran the chess hour, peered over her shoulder. "So? Are we keeping chess?"
Priscila tapped the numbers. "Chess has had three children for two months. The cards say it's 'fine.' Homework help has fourteen, and quiz scores went up from the last month."
"That's harsh on chess."
"Not stopping it yet. Let's try it on Saturday morning for one month instead. If it's still three, we stop and put you on homework help."
Ulla sighed, then smiled. "Fair. You've got the numbers."

Vidya, sit, let me tell you about your Nilesh Chacha at twenty-five. I worked at the bank all day and ran a night school for mill workers' children from seven to ten. Three months of that. I ate dinner at midnight, and I was so proud of myself.

You asked for an update on the Sunday science club before renewing your support, so here is the honest version.

I wanted ninety in physics finals. So I sat with last year's paper. Seventy marks theory. Mechanics carries about twenty-three, electricity about eighteen, optics fourteen, and so on. I asked myself, where am I losing? Mechanics I'm fine. Electricity I was getting maybe half.

"Product company, associate role, by next July," Rajni said, pointing at her notebook in the canteen. "Working back: offer in May, interviews March, shortlist in January, portfolio by December, internship this summer."
Lalit read it. "That's really neat. What's the first step?"
"Build skills."
"Which skills?"
"You know. Design thinking. Some data. Product sense."
"And this week?"
Rajni laughed. "This week I'm doing the plan."
Two months later, the summer internship list came out. Every listing asked for a small case study or a project link.
Lalit found her by the notice board. "Do you have anything to send?"
Rajni stared at the list. "I have a very good plan." Her voice cracked. "I don't have a single project."
"Let's pick one this weekend," Lalit said. "One. Small."

qa.q: When did the summer internship list come out?
qa.a: It came out two months later.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when her voice cracked at the notice board?
qa.a: She was shocked and ashamed, realising her neat plan had never produced a single project to send.

qa.q: What would you change first in Rajni's plan?
qa.a: I would turn "build skills" into one small project with a date this week, since every later step depends on having something to show.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Rajni's plan from the start?
qa.a: Lalit sees it looks tidy but notices the first step is vague, which is why Lalit keeps asking "which skills" and "this week".

grounding: It shows a final-year student whose backward plan to a product-company job looks neat while its first step stays vague, costing an internship chance.

subtopic: Working backward from the goal
subtype: Approach: assumes only the last step is known and chains backwards [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Lalremsiami, and last year I had the most beautiful career plan in my hostel.
Goal: analyst at a product company. Before that: pass the case interview. Before that: get shortlisted. Before that: a strong resume. Before that: "get good at SQL and statistics." I drew it as a staircase on chart paper and stuck it above my bed. Noor, my roommate, said it looked like a poster from a coaching centre.
Every step had a date except the bottom one. "Get good" never became a course, a book or a number of hours. I kept polishing the top steps, reading interview tips, practising my introduction.
In October the campus test had forty minutes of SQL. I solved two of eight questions.
Now when I plan backwards, I stop at the bottom and ask: what, exactly, will I do tomorrow morning?

qa.q: How many SQL questions did Lalremsiami solve in the campus test?
qa.a: Lalremsiami solved two of eight questions.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami probably feel after the October test?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt crushed and foolish, since the plan had looked beautiful but the one vague step was exactly what the test checked.

qa.q: What else could Lalremsiami have done with the bottom step, and why?
qa.a: The bottom step could have become a specific course with weekly hours, so progress could be seen long before October.

qa.q: How might Noor have seen the staircase above the bed?
qa.a: Noor saw it as a neat poster, which suggests it looked impressive from outside while the real work had not started.

grounding: It shows a final-year student whose tidy backward chain to a product-company job hides a vague first step, which costs them in the campus test.
